text: And moreover, we will also assume that the sequence is something like integers where we
can talk of one value being less than another value.
So, the values can be ordered with respect to each other.
So, we already saw that we can keep such sequences in two different ways as arrays and
as lists.
And depending on whether we keep it as arrays or lists, the way we can access the elements
differ is different.
So, the first question we might ask is whether searching makes a difference in a list
versus an array.
And the second question we might ask is is there some importance to how the values are
arranged in the sequence?
Does it help if they are in ascending or descending order?
Or does it not matter?
Is it equally the same to search for something in a randomly collected collection of values,
randomly ordered collection of values or when it is structured in some particular way?
So, in the unsorted case, we have no choice basically.
We have a sequence A which runs from 0 to n minus 1.
So, we must look at all the values because we have no idea where k may be.
So, a systematic way to do it is to start with the position 0 and just scan all the way
to n minus 1.
So, we have this loop here which scans and the scan either terminates when you reach the
end without finding it or when at some position i, we find that a i is equal to k.
And then depending on that, we either say that it is found in which case we return the
position or we have reached i equal to n which means we have gone beyond a n minus 1.
And so, we return not 1, minus 1 which is an invalid position, we indicate that it is
not found.
So, we saw before that the worst case actually happens when k is not an element of a.
That k does not come in a, we have to scan a 0 to a n minus 1 in order to determine that
k is not there because we have no evidence in advance which position is likely to be at.
So, this means that in the worst case, searching for an element in an unsorted area takes
linear time.
And of course, it does not matter now whether it is an array or a list because in a list
we could also linear time start from the first element and follow the links all the way
to the end.
In an array, we start with a 0 and go all the way to a n minus 1 both of them take linear
time.
On the other hand, if the sequence is sorted and in particular if it is an array, we can
be a little more intelligent.
So, what we know is that the values are say in ascending order.
So, if we probe the value in the middle and check this is this equal to k.
If the value that we have is equal to k of course, we have found it.
If it is smaller than the value here, then we only need to search in this half.
And if it is larger than we need to search in this half.
Now this is something that we intuitively do all the time.
This is how we look for say words in a dictionary or when we play 20 questions.
We try to ask questions about the age of a person, then we will say is this person less
than 40 is this person greater than 65 and so on.
So, this is something we know intuitively but we can formalize it.
So, we take the midpoint of the range we are searching for.
If the midpoint is a value that we want, we have found it.
Otherwise, we depending on the value we are looking for and what the value is at the
midpoint, we search either the bottom half or the top half.
So, this has a name which many of you may already know and this is called binary search.
So, here is a simple recursive algorithm for binary search.

text: Right.
The recurrence is just an expression for the time in terms of smaller values of the same
expression.
So, the base case is that when we have t of n, we mean the time taken to search in a list
or an array actually of size n.
Right.
So, t of 0 is 1.
So, if we have an empty array, we have nothing to do and t of n in general is one step to
find and compare.
So, this one is actually a constant number of steps to compare with the mid point and
decide to go up, down and all that.
So, those operations plus the time taken to search whichever half we focus on.
The left half or the right half.
Remember that if we look at the left half, we are never going to look at the right half
again.
So, one way to solve such a recurrence is to unwind it.
So, we have t n is 1 plus t n by 2.
So, we take n by 2 and we do n by 2 divided by 2 and rather than write it as n by 4, we
write as n by 2 square.
And this is because now if I do it one more time it is 1 plus 1 plus 1 divided by 2 cube
and so on.
In general, you can see that if I do it k times, then I am going to have k 1s here.
So, if I do 3 times l i 1 plus 1 plus 1 plus t n by 2 to 3 or 4 plus t n by 2 to 4 and
so on.
So, after k steps, I have k plus t of n by 2 to the k.
Now, when n by 2 to the k becomes 1, at the next step, I am going to get t of 0.
So, when does this become 1, when n is 2 to the k, in other words, when k is log 2 of
n.
So, when I get log 2 of n, then this is become t of 1 and at the next step, this is going
to become 1 plus t of 0.
So, this is going to be log n 1s and so, overall the complexity of binary search is just
order of log n.
